status: Primary-source research, strict editorial/key review, content/source/audio/preservation/browser/build and production offline gates passed; native review pending.
method: Inspected publishers’ own full teaching pages. Read Ishide 2011, 表現研究 93, pages 1–10 (full PDF text and rendered pages 2/9). The Meiji record supplies the researcher’s 2008 abstract; its full paper was not available and is not claimed inspected. Original stories, scenes and examples; editorial course placement is not an official JLPT assignment.

points.form: Past-event sequence and shifts to a scene’s immediate viewpoint
points.formation: Past/non-past endings participate in narration; temporal expressions, perception and narrative context determine the event sequence.
points.teachingChoice: Distinguish the university promise, present café reading and unfinished outcome. A brief 降っている sentence keeps the café viewpoint; it does not jump to the learner’s present day.
points.sourceCaution: Ishide analyses Sanshirō and Michikusa. Its discussion does not justify a universal equation of past with objectivity or non-past with emotion. IMABI’s significant-moment section supports context-sensitive narration, not a complete tense theory.

points.form: Plain quotation + と + 思った / 思っていた
points.formation: Plain quoted clause; noun and な-adjective complete predicates take だ. Past thinking does not mechanically set the embedded event’s time.
points.teachingChoice: Named thinkers initially mistake a note’s writer or the old shop’s identity. Later observed events correct the thought; silent 心の中で is explicit.
points.sourceCaution: Bunpro’s N4 label is editorial. Tofugu distinguishes impression from deliberation; this lesson concerns spontaneous character thoughts, not a blanket prohibition on third-person thought in narrated fiction.

points.form: Narrative のだった and conversational recalled んだった
points.formation: Plain clause + のだった; noun/な-adjective non-past + なのだった. The clause can be past or non-past.
points.teachingChoice: The bookmark makes a prior promise significant. Examples contrast a discovered fact and a departure still ahead of the narrative viewpoint; no mandatory literary suffix is taught.
points.sourceCaution: IMABI separately explains recalled/regretted conversational use and significant moments in writing. The researcher’s 2008 abstract contrasts four narrative forms in Yukiguni; only the abstract is used, not an invented account of the full paper.

points.form: ていく / てくる from a narrative reference point
points.formation: て-form + いく / くる; past ていった / てきた. Direction, developing perception or temporal change depends on the reference point.
points.teachingChoice: Laughter reaches the characters; the shop light recedes when they walk away. Earlier constructions are applied to advanced reading, without forcing every case into literal travel.
points.sourceCaution: Bunpro tags these N4. Coto’s movement/change illustrations are explanatory models, not a rule that every perception verb or narrated sentence must use one suffix.

editorialReview.sceneChoice: Friends rediscover an unfinished book and a former bakery now used as a bookshop. Supplementary literary vocabulary is kept in the study list instead of being forced into their talk.
editorialReview.remaining: Whole N2 core review after unit 16 and independent native sentence/listening review.

uninspected: The full 2008 paper on narrative のだった was not accessible; only the author’s own abstract was inspected.
